title: The one line you can win on
summary: Learn the summary speech, the last minute where you drop everything except the argument you are actually winning, then run a whole format against the machine and score it yourself on a real ballot.
materials: a sheet turned landscape for the flow, ruled the way week 3 taught it
the 2 minute and 1 minute sand timers, and the call bell
a second phone for the 90 second reply, run by the grown up
a ballot sheet, ruled by hand on one page
laptop with the AI, used with a grown up in the room

steps.title: Collapse to your best
steps.body:
The summary is the last speech, and it is one minute long. Almost everybody spends their first summaries saying everything again, faster. That loses, every time, and here is why.

At the end of a round the judge is holding a ballot with one box on it that decides things: who won, and in one sentence, why. The summary's only job is to write that sentence for them. A minute spent racing through six points writes nothing. A minute spent on one point writes the sentence.

So: of everything said in the whole round, pick the one argument you are still winning, and spend the entire minute there. It is the same move as a summit day. You do not climb every line up the face. You look at the mountain, you pick the one clean line, and you commit to it, and committing is what makes it work.

Three parts to a summary that lands. Name the one thing: this debate comes down to whether practice changes you or only changes what you can do. Show you won it: what they said, what you said back, and why yours is still standing. Then say why that decides the motion, not just the point.

And say out loud what you are dropping. Dropping something on purpose looks like control. Dropping it by accident looks like forgetting, and a judge cannot tell the difference unless you tell them.

The trap is choosing the argument you like best instead of the one you are winning. Those are different arguments more often than you would think, and only the flow can tell you which is which. Your favourite point lives in your head. The point you are winning lives in the right hand column, in the row where their answer was thin.

Tonight is the first time you run the whole format end to end, against the machine, all four speeches in the order week 1 set out: the opening constructive, the minute of questions, the ninety second reply, and the last word. A grown up stays in the room, runs the timers and helps neither side. The motion is practice changes who you are. You write both cases first and only then choose which one you are arguing, so neither one can be written lazily.

And carry the question into your recording: does practising something change who you are? You have run the same three tracks for seven weeks, and last week you made the same thing over and over until there was a pile of it. You are not a bystander in this argument. You are the evidence, on either side.

steps.title: Three summaries, three different lines
steps.body:
Ask the AI, with a grown up nearby, for a two minute constructive arguing for the motion practice changes who you are. Exactly three points, each with a claim and one reason, read at normal speaking speed rather than dumped on the screen. Flow it live in the left column, three numbered rows, the way week 3 taught it. Do not read ahead.

Now write three summaries, each one minute, each collapsing to a different single point. Number one spends the whole minute on their first point. Number two spends it on their second. Number three on their third. Each summary must name what it is dropping and why.

Deliver all three, standing, with the minute timer running each time. The timer is the referee you share, so finishing inside it is part of the job.

Then rank them and say why the winner won. The reason has to come off the flow, not off a feeling: point at the row where their answer was thinnest. That row, not your favourite row, is where the round is actually won.
checklist: The AI's constructive was flowed live, three numbered rows, before a single summary was written
Three summaries were written, each spending its whole minute on a different one of their points
Each summary said out loud what it was dropping
All three were delivered standing and inside the minute timer
I ranked them afterwards and gave a reason I could point at on the flow

steps.title: Rule the ballot, and build both cases
steps.body:
The ballot is one sheet, ruled by hand, four boxes with room to write in each:

1. Who answered the other side's best point, and what did they actually say?
2. Who backed a claim with something checkable, and what was it?
3. Who was easier to follow, and where exactly did the other one lose you?
4. Who won, and the one sentence why.

That sheet is what a judge fills in, so it is also the list of things worth doing. Read it once before you speak, every round, forever.

Now both cases, written before you choose. Whichever one you pick, the machine argues the other, so a case written lazily is a case that comes back at you. One sentence each, at full strength, steelman rule standing.

Strongest for: doing a thing over and over changes what you can do, what you notice without trying, and what your hands reach for before you decide anything. Seven weeks in, you hear a wrong note in an argument that you would have walked past in week 1, and a person who notices different things is a different person.

Strongest against: a habit is something you have, not something you are. Practice changes your hands and leaves you behind them, and the proof is that you can stop tomorrow and the person who stops is still you, unmistakably, with the same name and the same opinions.

Write both, then choose, and say out loud why you chose it. Whichever side you take, argue it like you mean it.
checklist: The ballot sheet has all four boxes with room to write in each
One strongest sentence is written for each side, and each would make its own side proud
I can say which box a judge is most likely to fill in first, and why

steps.title: Record it
steps.prompt: Record the whole format in one take if you can: the 2 minute constructive, the 1 minute of questions, the 90 second reply and the 1 minute last word, with the timers where the camera can see or hear them. Then hold the ballot up and read your own score out loud, including the sentence in the last box, even if the sentence goes against you. Finish by answering this week's question in your own words: does practising something change who you are?
